title: How a Texas Roof Claim Actually Goes
description: You call the carrier, an adjuster writes a scope, and the check often arrives in two pieces. Here is the sequence, without the driveway speech.
html:
A roof claim is a contract conversation with your insurance company. The roofer is not the insurance company. Anyone who says otherwise is about to ask you to sign something you should read twice.

The sequence that actually happens

  • You report the date of the storm and what you can see. Have photos ready.
  • The carrier sends an adjuster, or a third party, to write a scope: what they believe is damaged and what they will pay.
  • A contractor can meet that adjuster. We do. Two people looking at the same bruise is better than a photo taken from the street.
  • You receive an estimate. On many replacement-cost policies the first check holds back depreciation. That money is released after the work is done and documented.

Whether you have replacement cost or actual cash value is written in the policy, under loss settlement. Read that page before you spend the first check. A roofer who promises “insurance will cover all of it” has not read your policy.

What the scope misses

Adjusters move fast after a hail day. They miss pipe boots, soft decking, and the slope you cannot see from the street. A supplement is a normal part of the process when the tear-off shows more than the scope. It is not a trick, and it is not guaranteed. We photograph what we open and send it while the deck is still visible.

Read any contract before you sign. You should not have to hand the entire claim over to a contractor to get the roof fixed. Core Four will meet the adjuster, write what we see, and let you decide.

A plain path through it

The insurance claim walkthrough is the version we hand homeowners: from the first leak to a signed scope, including the holdback. Our insurance claims page is the same work, with a crew attached.
